findings.message: Backtracking is required for the best endings. 'pick-the-lock' (threshold) needs both lock-pick (only from shop-pick) and flood-stamp (only from alley-clue). No single forward path visits both shop-pick and alley-clue. The only way is start > shop > shop-pick > gathering > 'gather-alley' > alley > alley-clue > gathering > drone-street (or the mirror order). That forces the reader to reread 'gathering' (draft lines 181-207, choices 'Ride back to Tam's shop' / 'Ride back to the dark alley') and, via the alley, pass a stop they may have seen. Endings 1 and 2 are only reachable this way. This is a route that goes back over pages already read to collect an item.

Continuity on short routes. ending-5 (line 433) says 'She walked back to Tam's shop. He gave her hot soup', and Tam says 'listen to the little voice'. A reader who went start > alley > gathering > lane never met Tam or had soup. The reader who skipped the alley never heard of Aunt Ila, yet ending-4 (line 413) says 'It was Aunt Ila' and 'the flood gate' with no setup. ending-3 (line 394) mentions Tam's shop shut, which is also unexplained on the alley route.

Validation brief check warns that 1 sentence exceeds the brief's 16-word limit (validation.r7.json brief.warnings). Likely the long sentences in dash-past line 253 ('A drone swung round, and its flash lit the whole street...') or ending-1 line 356. Literacy reviewer should confirm.

lockedHint on 'pick-the-lock' (line 286) tells the reader what is needed but not where to find it. With the backtracking problem above, a reader who locked out has no pointer to the shop or alley. Consider hinting at the places. Fair, but weak.

'chill' reads as forced. In 'start', 'a chill sat on the handlebars' is an odd image. In 'dash-past', 'A chill ran over the handlebars, but her tyre held' is a non sequitur, because a chill has no link to the tyre, and a reader may stumble on the meaning. Suggest a natural use such as 'The rain was cold and she felt a chill' to narrative-designer.

Several set words appear only once in the story text, on one branch only: 'lunch' and 'sack' (shop), 'chase' (drone-street), 'much' (shop-pick), 'shot' (drone-street). The set totals pass, but these words get little repetition. The plan wanted two or more placements per word. Consider a second natural use of each, for example 'lunch' or 'much' at Tam's or in an ending, so the reader meets them again.

'tyre' (dash-past) has an irregular, British spelling and is not a decodable word, though the rest of the story uses it consistently ('grey', 'tyre'). It is the only odd spelling in an otherwise regular passage. Consider 'wheel' or 'tire' for a dyslexic reader, or keep it and accept it as a tricky word.

findings.message: Skills practised: Reading this story practises decoding closed-syllable words (bag, lock, mask, dash), sh words (shop, shade, flash) and ch words (chip, chill, lunch) in running text and in choice labels, plus -ing endings (blinking, pounding, watching). The reader sequences events across branches (gathering's 'First came the cab stand. Then came the shop or the alley. Now came the crossing', and Nine's 'First the gate, then the track, then the far light'), infers who to trust from clues (the flood stamp, Vex's grey mask, Tam's warning to 'check what they tell you') and works out new words such as broker, courier and drone from context and the glossary. The branching itself rewards checking evidence before acting, which keeps comprehension and inference central rather than incidental.

Word sets meet their minimums on r9 (literacy.r9): closed-syllable-words 43/10, sh-words 28/8, ch-words 28/8. Every listed word appears (no missingWords) and literacy.r9.json's word-sets-on-every-route check passes: each set appears on the shortest route to all five endings (closed-syllable 16-22 per route, sh 12-14, ch 8-10). By spelling, every word-set word carries its declared pattern with no conceptMismatches: cab, bag, pick, lock, mask, sack, dash, hack are closed syllables (one vowel, ends in a consonant); shop, shade, shot, shut, flash, shell contain sh; chip, chase, chill, much, lunch, chain contain ch. All four target concepts are present in running text: closed-syllable 595 tokens, digraph-sh 63, digraph-ch 38, suffix-ing 21.

The four single-choice fixes from revision-notes.r9.md read naturally and keep the word sets intact rather than diluting them. shop-pick's new line 'She could duck into its shade, or ride on to the crossing' reuses 'shade' (sh-words) in prose, not just the choice label. hide-shade's new choice label itself, 'Wave the drone down and give up the bag', reuses 'bag' (closed-syllable) as reading, per the Word Weave Plan's rule that choice labels count. alley-clue's new shortcut to drone-street and dash-past's new fork to hide-shade add a back lane and a shaded doorway without removing any existing sentence, so nothing that previously carried a word-set word was cut. Because climax-gate still requires both lock-pick (from shop-pick) and the flood-stamp clue (from alley-clue), every route to endings 1 and 2 still passes through those two passages regardless of which shortcut a reader takes, so the richest sh/ch/closed-syllable passages are not skippable on the way to the 'best' endings.

Age fit (10 to 13): average sentence length is 7.4 words, no sentence exceeds the 16-word limit the brief sets, and the new sentences added in r9 (e.g. 'Ahead, the street forked.', 'Nine warned that more drones might wait at the bridge.') are all well under it. The longest passage (start, 148 words) is still reasonable for this age. Peril stays mild and consistent with the brief's 'avoid' list across all five endings, including the newly reachable ending-5 route through hide-shade ('Nobody was hurt'). Tricky vocabulary (broker, courier, crouched, eased) is supported by context and the four glossary entries; the new text in r9 introduces no new unsupported vocabulary.

This did not block r9 (weave-comparison.r9.json only compares set totals, and it passes), but the plan and draft still disagree word-for-word. Recommend the orchestrator regenerate the plan so it names 'chill', not 'patch', and have the parent confirm that substitution.

Unresolved from the r8 review: in dash-past, 'A drone swung round, and its flash lit the whole street. The chain on her bike sang as she turned. A chill ran down her back, but her wheel held.' still joins 'A chill ran down her back' and 'her wheel held' with 'but', though fear and a wheel holding are not in contrast. This passage was touched in r9 (a new fork was appended after it) but this sentence itself was left as in r8. Suggest narrative-designer split it, e.g. 'A chill ran down her back. Her wheel held.'

Two set words still get only one occurrence each in running prose: 'shot' (drone-street: 'It shot a white flash over the wet street, back and forth') and 'chase' (drone-street: 'They were on a chase for any courier with a sealed chip'). Set totals pass comfortably without more repetition, but a second natural use of each (drone-street is read on every route, so any addition there reaches every reader) would give the reader more practice with these two words specifically. Not a blocker for this revision, which was scoped to the graph fix.

Limits of this review: the analyzer detects spelling, not sound, so its counts include some false positives (for example 'the' and 'she' under the th/sh digraph counts, and silent-e or vowel-team words that also happen to contain 'sh' or 'ch', such as 'shade', 'chase' and 'chain'). It does not judge decodability, vocabulary level or story quality, and I have not tested the story with a child or checked sound-level pronunciation. 'grey' (British spelling) and the names Ila and Nine are not decodable by the stated target patterns and should be treated as tricky/sight words. findings.message: The new 'dash-duck' choice added to fix dash-past's single-choice flag reuses 'hide-shade' for a context it was not written for, producing a continuity break. dash-past's new fork text (lines 276, 286-290) sets up 'a shaded doorway' and has Mara duck in 'to catch her breath' after she has already lost the drones ('the hum fell behind her', line 274). hide-shade's text, written for the drone-street entry, instead opens with an active, close drone pass ('The drones passed so close that the wind from them stirred her hair. Their flash slid over the shelter and moved on.', line 248) and refers to 'the shelter' -- an object only ever named by drone-street's 'bus shelter' choice label (line 233), never by dash-past's 'doorway' wording. A reader who takes drone-street > dash-past > dash-duck > hide-shade meets an object with no antecedent on their route and a drone threat that contradicts the escape they just read two paragraphs earlier. This is a new defect introduced by this revision's fix, not present before dash-past linked into hide-shade. The other three r9 fixes (shop-pick's 'pick-skip-alley', alley-clue's 'clue-shortcut', hide-shade's 'shade-give-up') are genuine, non-filler branch points that fit the setting and reuse target word-set vocabulary ('pick', 'shade' in shop-pick; the sh/ch word sets are otherwise untouched) without this kind of mismatch.

Carried over from the r8 QA pass (not addressed in this content-only revision): 'gathering' still labels choices 'Ride back to Tam's shop' and 'Ride back to the dark alley' (lines 206, 211), which presume a visit that not every route makes (e.g. start > alley > alley-leave > gathering never visits the shop; start > shop > leave-shop > gathering never visits the alley). Neutral wording ('Ride to...') would fit all routes.

Carried over from the r8 QA pass (not addressed in this content-only revision): at climax-gate, Mara picks the lock and 'eased the gate shut behind her' (line 332), then Vex 'stepped out of the fog' already on the bridge (line 334) with no explanation of how he got past the shut, locked gate, even though a cab engine growling behind her at threshold (line 300) implies he followed her there.
